# The Orphan Sense

Consider how difficult it is to describe the smell of rain falling on hot pavement. There is a word for it—petrichor, coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists who studied the phenomenon—but the word is a label, not a description. It tells you the name of the box, not what's inside. For our other senses, language offers adjectives that stand on their own. Color: crimson, slate, gold. Sound: shrill, muffled, brassy. Touch: velvety, gritty, damp. But ask someone what rain-on-asphalt smells like and they will say it smells like rain on asphalt. They might mention dust, or lightning, or worms. Smell is the one sense we describe almost entirely by reference to sources, as if the nose were just an index of things.

That's strange, because of all the senses, smell has the most direct line to what we care about. Sight and sound and touch route their signals through the thalamus, the brain's central switchboard, before sending them onward for processing. Smell skips the switchboard. Olfactory signals run nearly straight into the amygdala and hippocampus—the seats of emotion and memory. This anatomy explains a familiar experience: a smell does not remind you of the past so much as drop you into it. The perfume of a stranger in an elevator can unhinge you in a way no melody quite can. Proust needed an entire madeleine, dipped in tea, to make the point; the point is that nobody weeps at the sight of a particular shade of blue, and everybody has been ambushed by a scent.

Part of the problem is words. Linguists who study perception have found that most of the world's languages have no abstract vocabulary for smell. English speakers say "smells like lemon," "smells like a bonfire"—always borrowing the name of a thing. But a handful of languages, such as Jahai, spoken in the Malay Peninsula, do have abstract smell terms, the way English has abstract color terms, and their speakers use them fluently and consistently. The lesson is uncomfortable and liberating at once: the deficit is in our vocabulary, not our noses.

Because the noses are remarkable. Humans have roughly four hundred kinds of olfactory receptors, and we are far better smellers than the old story of our inadequacy suggests. We can follow a scent trail through a field (in one small study, volunteers crawled a chocolate-scented path on all fours and mostly stayed on it). We can detect geosmin—the compound made by soil bacteria that gives rain its smell, and beets their earthiness—at concentrations measured in parts per trillion, a sensitivity bordering on the absurd. We simply never built a culture worthy of the instrument.

We know this in our bones, and 2020 proved it. When COVID-19 stripped millions of people of their sense of smell, the losses were strangely specific and strangely devastating. Food turned to texture, because what we call taste is mostly smell. Lovers' skin became anonymous. Smoke, gas, spoiled milk—the nose's urgent telegrams—went silent. Some people recovered; some developed parosmia, a condition in which everything smells wrong, coffee like sewage, a horror with no visual equivalent. People who had never once thought about olfaction wrote elegies for it. The absence made the organ visible.

What the pandemic revealed, though, is not only that smell matters, but that we had been systematically exiling it. Modern public life is a long war on odor. We deodorize, sanitize, mask, and scent everything that remains with a borrowed "clean" smell, as though neutrality were achievable. The war began, in part, with miasma theory, the old belief that disease traveled on foul air; cities scrubbed, and when germ theory arrived to explain sickness properly, the scrubbing continued out of habit and class anxiety. The historian Alain Corbin traced the West's turn against smell in *The Foul and the Fragrant*, and the turn never fully reversed. We left ourselves one indulgence—perfume—expensive, bottled, permitted. Meanwhile other cultures built entire arts around scent. In Japan, the incense ceremony of kōdō treats smelling as listening; participants "hear" the incense and play games matching subtle blends to chapters of *The Tale of Genji*. Imagine being moved to build a cathedral for the ear and leaving the nose to stand in the doorway.

Here is the thing, though: it is never too late to learn the language. The nose adapts ferociously—step into someone's house and you are hit by its smell; within minutes you are blind to it, which is why your own home, and for that matter your own body, smell like nothing to you. Adaptation is a kind of mercy, and also a kind of amnesia. Attention undoes it, briefly. So: one smell a day. The inside of your wrist in the afternoon. The hallway of the building where you grew up, if you can get back there, and how it is both exactly the same and not at all. The head of someone you love, which is the part of love no one mentions and everyone knows—the specific, unreproducible weather of another person's hair. Babies know their mothers by smell within days; mothers know their babies; the nose files all of this away without asking permission and keeps the records for decades.

It is worth being honest about what this record is for. Photographs can be scanned and voices recorded, but the smell of a person's apartment cannot be archived. It dies with them, and with the building. This is why people open a coat left in a closet and sit down on the stairs. The sense we never learned to describe is the one that keeps what nothing else can hold.

Outside, if it has rained, the pavement will be doing its ancient thing: bacteria in the soil exhale geosmin, the falling water lifts it, and the air fills with a signal our species can detect at a trillion-to-one dilution, carrying no information and all of it. We have no words for it, really. We only named it after the fact, the way you name someone you have already fallen in love with.

That's strange, because of all the senses, smell has the most direct line to what we care about. Sight and sound and touch route their signals through the thalamus, the brain's central switchboard, before sending them onward for processing. Smell skips the switchboard. Olfactory signals run nearly straight into the amygdala and hippocampus—the seats of emotion and memory. This anatomy explains a familiar experience: a smell does not remind you of the past so much as drop you into it. The perfume of a stranger in an elevator can unhinge you in a way no melody quite can. People who had never once thought about olfaction wrote elegies for it. The absence made the organ visible.
